items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “A limited-capacity system that holds and processes information while a task is being carried out”?
items.answer: Working memory
items.markingKey: Working memory: a limited-capacity system that holds and processes information while a task is being carried out. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Doing two tasks at once can reduce performance. Reason (R): Working memory has a limited capacity. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Limited capacity explains why dual tasks interfere. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Daydreaming improves concentration on a boring task. Reason (R): Daydreaming uses the central executive. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: A is false: daydreaming uses resources and impairs concentration; R is true. [1]

items.stem: Kenji, a student in Seoul, often finds that during long online lectures their mind wanders to plans for the weekend. Use Andrade’s findings to suggest one way Kenji could improve concentration.
items.answer: Doodle (for example shading shapes) while listening, which may stop daydreaming and improve recall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark doodling; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Kwame, a student in Santiago, often finds that during long online lectures their mind wanders to plans for the weekend. (a) Identify the cognitive process that Kwame is experiencing. (b) Use Andrade’s findings to suggest one way Kwame could improve concentration.
items.answer: (a) Daydreaming (mind-wandering), a lapse of attention. (b) Doodle (for example shading shapes) while listening, which may stop daydreaming and improve recall.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark doodling; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Sofia, a student in Toronto, often finds that during long online lectures their mind wanders to plans for the weekend. (a) Use Andrade’s findings to suggest one way Sofia could improve concentration. (b) Explain, using working memory, why daydreaming could reduce what Sofia remembers.
items.answer: (a) Doodle (for example shading shapes) while listening, which may stop daydreaming and improve recall. (b) Daydreaming uses central executive resources, leaving less capacity for processing the lecture, so less is encoded.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark doodling; 1 mark reason [2] (b) 1 mark resources used; 1 mark less encoding [2]

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “The component of working memory that directs attention and coordinates the other components”.
items.answer: Central executive
items.markingKey: Central executive: the component of working memory that directs attention and coordinates the other components. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “The working memory model says that the phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad are controlled by the central executive.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. The central executive allocates attention to the slave systems.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how doodling might help concentration, according to Andrade.
items.answer: A boring task leads to low arousal and daydreaming, which uses the central executive and distracts from the task; doodling uses little capacity but keeps arousal up and stops daydreaming, so more attention stays on the message.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: boredom/daydreaming uses resources; 1 mark: doodling prevents daydreaming; 1 mark: more attention to task [3]

items.stem: Evaluate Andrade’s (2010) study of doodling and concentration, including a discussion of standardisation.
items.answer: Strength (standardisation): Every participant heard the same pre-recorded 2.5-minute telephone message in the same monotonous voice and received the same instructions, so the procedure was consistent and replicable. Strength (usefulness): The finding that doodling improved recall by about 29% suggests that doodling could help people concentrate in boring situations such as long lectures or meetings. Weakness (ecological validity): Shading shapes on a sheet is not the same as spontaneous doodling, and the message was artificial, so the task may not represent everyday listening. Weakness (ethics): Participants were mildly deceived: they were not told that there would be a memory test, so they had to be debriefed afterwards. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Describe the procedure of Andrade’s study.
items.answer: Forty participants were randomly allocated to a doodling or control group. All listened to a 2.5-minute monotonous telephone message about a party and wrote down the names of people coming. The doodling group shaded shapes while listening. Afterwards there was a surprise test of names and places mentioned.
items.markingKey: 1 mark allocation/groups; 1 mark message and monitoring; 1 mark shading; 1 mark surprise recall [4]

items.stem: Freya replicated Andrade’s study in Istanbul. 6 participants shaded shapes while listening to a boring telephone message and 6 participants just listened. All then had a surprise test of the names and places mentioned (out of 16). Table: Names and places recalled (out of 16) — Doodling: 6, 9, 8, 7, 6, 9. Control (no doodling): 4, 6, 4, 4, 3, 4. The standard deviation for the doodling condition was 1.38 and for the control (no doodling) condition was 0.98. Explain what these values show.
items.answer: The doodling condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the condition with the larger spread; 1 mark: explains that a larger SD means scores are more spread around the mean [2]

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Andrade’s (2010) study of doodling and concentration. Include at least one point about controls.
items.answer: Strength (controls): Participants were randomly allocated to the doodling and control groups and all had just completed another study, so both groups were similarly bored; differences in recall are more likely to be due to doodling. Strength (usefulness): The finding that doodling improved recall by about 29% suggests that doodling could help people concentrate in boring situations such as long lectures or meetings. Weakness (generalisability): The sample of 40 was mostly female (35 women) and recruited from one research panel in Cambridge, so the findings may not generalise to men or other populations. Weakness (ecological validity): Shading shapes on a sheet is not the same as spontaneous doodling, and the message was artificial, so the task may not represent everyday listening. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: ‘Doodling helps people to concentrate.’ To what extent do you agree? In your answer, you may refer to usefulness, ecological validity and working memory.
items.answer: Arguments for: Andrade found doodlers recalled 29% more information from a boring telephone message than controls. Doodling may reduce daydreaming, which uses working memory resources. Arguments against: Shading set shapes is not real doodling, so the finding may not generalise. Doodling may distract from tasks that need visual attention. The sample was small and mostly female. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: In a replication of Andrade (2010) in Kathmandu, participants were randomly allocated to a doodling group or a control group, listened to a 2.5-minute message and then recalled names and places (maximum 16). Table: Names and places recalled (out of 16) — Doodling: 8, 5, 7, 6, 7, 6, 9, 9. Control (no doodling): 7, 7, 5, 6, 6, 6, 8, 5. (a) Calculate the median score for the control (no doodling) condition. (b) Calculate the range of scores for each condition. (c) To what extent do these results support the prediction that participants who doodle while listening will recall more names and places than participants who only listen? Use the data in your answer. (d) Explain why a repeated measures design might have been used instead, and one problem this would cause.
items.answer: (a) 6 (b) Doodling: 4; control (no doodling): 3. (c) Mean for doodling = 7.1 and control (no doodling) = 6.3; the direction of the difference matches the prediction, but the scores in the two conditions overlap (ranges 4 and 3) and the sample is small (n = 8 per condition), so the results only partly support it; a statistical test would be needed to show the difference is significant. items.stem: A researcher in Nairobi is interested in how often students doodle in lessons. Plan an observation to test this. Your plan must include: the sampling technique, how inter-rater reliability will be checked, ethical issues and behavioural categories.
items.answer: Method: an observation. Structured observation with operationalised behavioural categories and time sampling; two observers to check inter-rater reliability; overt or covert as appropriate. Variables: behaviour: doodling; categories: doodling, note-taking, looking at the teacher. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Nairobi, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: “Andrade’s (2010) study of doodling and concentration has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including ethics in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (demand characteristics): The recall test was a surprise, so participants could not deliberately try to remember the message, making recall a more valid measure of incidental memory. Strength (usefulness): The finding that doodling improved recall by about 29% suggests that doodling could help people concentrate in boring situations such as long lectures or meetings. Weakness (ethics): Participants were mildly deceived: they were not told that there would be a memory test, so they had to be debriefed afterwards. Weakness (demand characteristics): Participants in the doodling group were asked to shade shapes, which might have suggested that doodling was being tested, and they may have tried harder. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Assess the view that doodling helps people to concentrate. In your answer, you may refer to usefulness and working memory.
items.answer: Arguments for: Andrade found doodlers recalled 29% more information from a boring telephone message than controls. Doodling may reduce daydreaming, which uses working memory resources. Arguments against: Shading set shapes is not real doodling, so the finding may not generalise. Doodling may distract from tasks that need visual attention. The sample was small and mostly female. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Evaluate Andrade’s (2010) study of doodling and concentration in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about usefulness.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): The finding that doodling improved recall by about 29% suggests that doodling could help people concentrate in boring situations such as long lectures or meetings. Strength (standardisation): Every participant heard the same pre-recorded 2.5-minute telephone message in the same monotonous voice and received the same instructions, so the procedure was consistent and replicable. Weakness (ethics): Participants were mildly deceived: they were not told that there would be a memory test, so they had to be debriefed afterwards. Weakness (demand characteristics): Participants in the doodling group were asked to shade shapes, which might have suggested that doodling was being tested, and they may have tried harder. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: What is meant by ‘working memory’?

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why doodling might be expected to make concentration worse. items.answer: (a) If doodling and listening compete for the same limited working memory resources (especially the central executive), doing both at once should reduce attention to the message. (b) Correct. The central executive allocates attention to the slave systems.

items.stem: “Andrade’s (2010) study of doodling and concentration has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including controls in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (standardisation): Every participant heard the same pre-recorded 2.5-minute telephone message in the same monotonous voice and received the same instructions, so the procedure was consistent and replicable. Strength (controls): Participants were randomly allocated to the doodling and control groups and all had just completed another study, so both groups were similarly bored; differences in recall are more likely to be due to doodling. Weakness (ethics): Participants were mildly deceived: they were not told that there would be a memory test, so they had to be debriefed afterwards. Weakness (ecological validity): Shading shapes on a sheet is not the same as spontaneous doodling, and the message was artificial, so the task may not represent everyday listening. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
